title: PDF Accessibility Preflight
user: People who publish PDFs for colleagues, students, or customers with low vision and need a quick, understandable check before sharing.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A knowledge worker gradually losing sight asks for tools that work across modern browser-based office apps; keyboard and voice control do not cover the workflow.
A feature request asks for built-in PDF accessibility testing and says accessible PDF production remains an ongoing challenge for government and education.

recurrence: Two independent 2025–26 communities identify accessibility as a workflow failure, not a cosmetic preference; low-vision users bear the cost at the moment a document is shared.
current_workaround: Run a full enterprise accessibility suite, manually inspect tags, or discover the problem only when a recipient cannot use the PDF.
incumbents_and_gap: Adobe Acrobat Pro and veraPDF are capable but technical or expensive; PDF editors do not provide a plain-language, recipient-oriented preflight for the small document sender.
smallest_useful_product: A local drag-and-drop web app that reports missing document language, title, bookmarks, tagged headings, alt-text candidates, reading-order red flags, and a sharable remediation checklist. Non-goals: automatic legal compliance certification, OCR, or a PDF editor.
success_measure: In a 30-day pilot, 70% of uploaded PDFs receive at least one correction before being sent and users complete the checklist in under five minutes.
monetization: freemium — an offline basic report earns trust; batch reports and branded team checklists can fund it.
constraints: Process documents entirely in-browser by default; clearly label heuristic findings; do not claim WCAG/PDF-UA conformance without a full validator; protect embedded PII.
why_distinct: It translates structural PDF checks into a small sender-facing handoff checklist rather than trying to be another document editor.

title: Code Proof
user: Engineers and technical writers producing long Markdown manuals who need to catch broken code blocks, wrapping, and internal links in the final PDF.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker tried md2pdf, Pandoc, and LaTeX but could not get a large code-heavy document to retain internal PDF links, syntax highlighting, and usable code wrapping.
A user requests Markdown-to-PDF code-block preservation because fenced JavaScript lost its newlines and rendered as a paragraph.

recurrence: Two independent conversion requests in 2025 identify the same high-severity failure: source Markdown looks correct while the delivered PDF is unusable.
current_workaround: Try several converters, tune LaTeX/print CSS by hand, and visually page through PDFs before release.
incumbents_and_gap: Pandoc, Quarto, md2pdf, and browser print pipelines convert Markdown; none makes a focused regression proof for links, code overflow, and language highlighting the primary artifact.
smallest_useful_product: A local CLI that renders Markdown through a chosen engine, checks PDF annotations and page geometry, flags overflowing/unhighlighted fenced blocks, and emits an HTML proof sheet. Non-goals: a Markdown editor, hosted conversion, or a replacement renderer.
success_measure: At least 80% of pilot document releases run the proof command, and it catches a release-blocking render defect in 20% or more of first runs.
monetization: free — CI and local documentation adoption matter more than gating a small verifier; paid support can follow if demand appears.
constraints: Do not execute embedded HTML/JavaScript with network access; sandbox renderer subprocesses; make checks engine-specific and reproducible.
why_distinct: The product verifies a PDF delivery contract instead of adding a competing Markdown-to-PDF renderer.

title: PDF Link Map
user: Operations and technical-document teams converting HTML or DOCX to PDF who need to know whether navigation survives the conversion.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN user calls wkhtmltopdf painful and asks for current open-source HTML-to-PDF options; replies emphasize browser rendering and tricky print CSS.
A user reports that a DOCX has clickable contents and lists of figures/tables, but PDF conversion leaves the latter links non-clickable.

recurrence: Different source formats and converters produce the same silent defect: the visible table of contents remains while navigation breaks.
current_workaround: Open the PDF and manually click a handful of links or wait for a reader complaint.
incumbents_and_gap: Puppeteer, wkhtmltopdf, LibreOffice, and unoconv render PDFs; their logs do not provide a source-to-destination link coverage map or a CI failure threshold.
smallest_useful_product: A CLI that accepts a PDF plus optional heading manifest, inventories internal/external annotations, validates destinations and duplicate anchors, and writes a clickable HTML map. Non-goals: PDF rendering, document authoring, or external-link crawling.
success_measure: A pilot team detects every deliberately broken TOC/list link in a fixture suite and adds the command to one release pipeline within 30 days.
monetization: one-time — specialist documentation QA is a durable local utility with no need to retain files.
constraints: Never dereference external links by default; parse malformed PDFs defensively; do not modify signed documents.
why_distinct: It treats link integrity as a testable handoff contract, independent of the converter that created the file.

title: Scan Reading Pack
user: Readers with scanned books or reports who need trustworthy selectable text and an audiobook-ready package while retaining page references to the original scan.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A reader wants scanned philosophy PDFs converted to text for notes and audiobooks; classic OCR makes mistakes and their only good workaround is sending page snippets to ChatGPT.
A PDF-to-Markdown request says image links without extracted image files make the conversion useless when images matter.

recurrence: Both requests expose that extraction must preserve a usable relationship to the source, not merely emit a text blob.
current_workaround: Run conventional OCR, copy pages into a chat model, or create text and images separately with no reliable page mapping.
incumbents_and_gap: OCRmyPDF, Tesseract, Adobe Scan, and PDF-to-Markdown tools extract content, but a compact reader-oriented pack with page anchors, confidence queues, and local audio export is uncommon.
smallest_useful_product: An offline desktop/PWA flow for image-only PDFs: OCR locally, produce Markdown/EPUB-like HTML with page anchors and extracted figures, queue low-confidence lines, and export SSML/plain text. Non-goals: cloud LLM correction, DRM removal, or hosting copyrighted books.
success_measure: In a pilot of 20 scanned documents, users correct fewer than 10 lines per 100 pages before exporting a pack and can jump from any text block back to its source page.
monetization: one-time — privacy-sensitive personal conversion is well suited to a paid offline desktop-quality utility.
constraints: Use local WASM/native OCR; warn users about copyright and private documents; keep original page coordinates; avoid claims of perfect transcription.
why_distinct: The valuable output is a verifiable reading package with source-page traceability, not an opaque AI transcription wrapper.

title: Import Transform Ledger
user: Implementation consultants and operations staff loading CSV data into business systems who need repeatable mapping, cleanup, and an audit trail without writing a bespoke script.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker names tedious template imports into Salesforce, Workday, and NetSuite—date formatting, code remapping, and aligning legacy data—and asks whether people rely on Excel, scripts, or Power Query.
A local-first finance app’s backlog separately calls for bank CSV column mapping, dedupe, categorization, and full CSV/JSON backup/restore.

recurrence: Independent enterprise-import and local-finance workflows require the same combination of column mapping, dedupe, transformation, and repeatability.
current_workaround: Use Excel/Power Query with undocumented edits, maintain fragile scripts, or hand-clean every new supplier export.
incumbents_and_gap: Power Query, OpenRefine, and ETL platforms are powerful; the gap is a tiny portable transform recipe that non-engineers can review, rerun, and attach to an import handoff.
smallest_useful_product: A local web app that compares source/target CSV headers, records mapping and deterministic transforms, previews rejects/duplicates, and exports a recipe plus output/checksum report. Non-goals: connecting to SaaS accounts, automatic semantic mapping, or a data warehouse.
success_measure: At least 60% of pilot imports are rerun from a saved recipe with zero manual spreadsheet edits, and every rejected row has an explicit reason.
monetization: one-time — consultants can buy a privacy-preserving field utility instead of another ongoing ETL subscription.
constraints: All processing local by default; recipes must be diffable JSON; support UTF-8/legacy encodings safely; never infer sensitive mappings with an LLM.
why_distinct: It makes a human-reviewed import recipe and rejection ledger the product, rather than another general spreadsheet or ETL service.

title: History Export Sentinel
user: People archiving or moving their browser history who need a cross-platform export they can verify is complete before an account or machine changes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN user asks why exporting/transferring data across online services remains impractical despite portability rights and describes it as technically difficult.
A feature request reports that browser-history export is macOS-only, has a Firefox SQLite error, and can silently generate an empty result.

recurrence: Data-portability friction appears at both the broad consumer level and the concrete browser-history export step; silent emptiness makes the risk severe.
current_workaround: Copy browser database files, run brittle shell scripts, or assume an export succeeded because a file was created.
incumbents_and_gap: Browser sync, ArchiveBox, and bookmark exporters preserve some data, but they do not offer a small cross-browser completeness report for a local history export.
smallest_useful_product: A local CLI that detects installed Chromium/Firefox profiles, copies databases safely, exports normalized JSON/CSV, and reports record/date ranges, locked-profile errors, and hashes. Non-goals: web-page archiving, cloud sync, or bypassing browser encryption.
success_measure: On a fixture set for Firefox and Chromium on three OSes, the tool either exports expected count/date ranges or emits a non-zero actionable failure; no silent empty export.
monetization: free — portability needs trust and interoperability; optional paid desktop packaging is plausible later.
constraints: Read copies only, never touch live browser databases; clearly handle profile encryption and OS permissions; history is highly sensitive and must never leave the device.
why_distinct: It is an export-verification utility, not another read-later service or browser-history visualizer.

title: Android Backup Coverage
user: Android owners who self-host or use multiple backup destinations and need proof that new photos and selected folders actually reached a second copy.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN user asks how to back up Android; replies split across Google backup, Termux/rsync, and older root-oriented tools.
A 33-reaction request asks for forced rescans and comparison against the remote folder because missing photo uploads recur and need daily detection.

recurrence: The backup question and a heavily supported rescan request converge on a missing capability: users cannot see coverage gaps before data loss.
current_workaround: Trust background upload, open a backup app periodically, compare folders manually, or write ad hoc rsync scripts.
incumbents_and_gap: Google One, Nextcloud, Immich, Syncthing, and rsync move files; they do not provide a destination-neutral, user-readable coverage receipt for selected Android folders.
smallest_useful_product: An Android app that inventories configured source folders, computes local file manifests, reads a user-selected destination manifest/share, highlights missing/late files, and schedules a visible verification reminder. Non-goals: a cloud-storage provider, hidden background uploads, or app-data backup bypasses.
success_measure: In a 60-day pilot, 95% of newly captured photos are marked verified within the user’s chosen window and every simulated missing upload is surfaced within 24 hours.
monetization: one-time — a local assurance layer should not tax storage volume or require account access.
constraints: Respect Android scoped-storage permissions and battery limits; do not claim to back up app-private data; manifests must be encrypted or local; make destination adapters opt-in.
why_distinct: It measures backup coverage across tools instead of competing to become the user’s next photo cloud.

title: Photo Delta Archive
user: Google Photos users who want a restorable, incremental local archive even when the provider API and Takeout workflow do not support it cleanly.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker finds Google Photos offers a one-off Takeout export but no incremental backup, and respondents describe manual Takeout or brittle headless-browser scripts.
rclone planned to remove Google Photos backup code because Google removed the scopes it depended on after March 2025.

recurrence: A direct request for incremental archival and a major sync tool losing API scope demonstrate a structural—not merely UX—gap.
current_workaround: Repeated full Takeout exports, fragile browser automation, or switching photo libraries and hoping the migration is complete.
incumbents_and_gap: Google Takeout, rclone, Immich, and photo clouds can export or host photos; the unresolved gap is a local archive ledger that understands repeated provider exports and verifies what changed.
smallest_useful_product: A desktop CLI that ingests successive user-downloaded Takeout archives, normalizes sidecars, de-duplicates by content plus metadata, builds a dated delta ledger, and verifies restore samples. Non-goals: scraping Google Photos, circumventing revoked APIs, or replacing the photo library.
success_measure: For two overlapping Takeout fixtures, it identifies 100% of additions/duplicates/metadata changes and produces a restore manifest without duplicate media files.
monetization: one-time — users making a provider-exit archive value an offline purchase over a new recurring photo service.
constraints: Only process files the user downloaded; metadata handling must preserve timezone/privacy; never automate login or evade provider controls; provide clear deletion options.
why_distinct: It works with sanctioned exports and produces an auditable delta, rather than pretending revoked APIs can be restored.

title: Restore Drill
user: Individuals and small teams with scripted backups who need a low-friction, repeatable proof that their backup can restore the files they care about.

evidence.quote_or_summary: People answering a personal backup-and-sync question describe layered setups—restic, rsync, Btrfs, NAS, and friends’ storage—rather than a simple confidence check.
A restic user runs read-data verification and encounters extensive damaged/duplicate pack output, illustrating that backup health can remain unknown until a check is attempted.

recurrence: Both personal backup practice and a real verification failure show that having several backup tools does not equal proven recovery.
current_workaround: Read backup job logs, run an occasional vendor-specific check, or attempt a full restore only during an emergency.
incumbents_and_gap: restic, Borg, Backblaze, NAS products, and cloud drives provide their own checks; a portable scheduler for small sampled restore drills and a human-readable receipt is missing.
smallest_useful_product: A local CLI that runs configured safe sample restores into a temporary directory, verifies hashes and selected application-open checks, records an immutable receipt, and alerts only on a failed or overdue drill. Non-goals: backup transport, credential vaulting, or full disaster-recovery orchestration.
success_measure: Pilot users complete a successful restore drill every 30 days; all injected corrupt/missing fixture cases fail loudly with a remediation hint.
monetization: free — transparent, local verification should integrate with existing backup choices; paid managed reminders are optional later.
constraints: Restore only into an explicitly created temporary target; use least-privilege repository credentials; never log file contents or passphrases; clean temporary output safely after verification.
why_distinct: It proves recovery through a small recurring drill instead of being another backup engine or dashboard.

title: Cold Storage Refresh Ledger
user: People keeping offline drives or archive media who need to know what to test, replace, and copy before media age turns into unrecoverable loss.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A user asks which long-term physical storage format is durable; replies stress 3-2-1 and the need to periodically check integrity and replace disks.
A request for a no-retry option explains that automatic retries can block backup scripts indefinitely after a repository/storage failure.

recurrence: Media longevity advice depends on recurring checks, while real backup automation can mask a failed destination through retries; both require explicit maintenance evidence.
current_workaround: Label disks by hand, remember approximate purchase dates, run scattered checksum commands, or discover a problem when an archive is needed.
incumbents_and_gap: Drive SMART tools, restic, and backup apps expose low-level status; none offers a small, media-agnostic calendar and signed manifest for offline archive refresh duties.
smallest_useful_product: A local CLI/PWA that records archive media, manifest hashes, last successful mount/read sample, planned refresh interval, and prints a one-page maintenance card. Non-goals: predicting drive failure, cloud backup, or managing encrypted contents.
success_measure: A 90-day pilot has 90% of enrolled media receive an on-time read sample and correctly escalates every overdue or unreadable test medium.
monetization: one-time — physical archive owners need durable records that do not depend on a hosted subscription.
constraints: Keep only metadata and hashes locally unless explicitly imported; do not overstate media-life predictions; support exportable, open JSON/CSV records.
why_distinct: It is a maintenance-and-evidence ledger for cold archives, not a duplicate-file finder or cloud storage product.

title: Cloud Exit Evidence
user: People keeping a local fallback for cloud files who need an evidence-backed answer to whether their physical copy is complete enough to rely on.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker wants an affordable physical copy of SaaS-synced cloud files in case the provider terminates them; replies warn that synchronization is not backup.
Google’s revocation of all-files access left Nextcloud Android auto-upload limited to photos/videos and custom folder backup restricted, creating an explicit coverage gap.

recurrence: The exit concern is not solved by merely syncing: platform permissions can silently exclude categories of files from the supposed local fallback.
current_workaround: Use a NAS, external drive, rclone, or vendor sync app and assume that the local folder is complete.
incumbents_and_gap: Synology, QNAP, rclone, cloud sync clients, and backup programs copy data; they rarely provide a provider-neutral inventory comparison that calls out unsupported paths and permissions.
smallest_useful_product: A local CLI that compares a cloud-provider export/listing or sync manifest with an offline destination, classifies coverage by folder/type/date, records excluded paths, and emits an exit-readiness report. Non-goals: downloading from accounts, acting as a sync daemon, or bypassing OS permissions.
success_measure: On a fixture with intentional permission exclusions and stale files, the report identifies all missing coverage categories and makes no claim of readiness until each is acknowledged or remediated.
monetization: free — provider portability reports need credibility and should not require surrendering credentials to a new service.
constraints: Read manifests/exports only; no credential storage in v1; distinguish backup from sync prominently; encrypt any saved manifests because paths can be sensitive.
why_distinct: It produces a falsifiable exit-readiness report across existing tools rather than becoming yet another cloud-sync client.

title: Calendar Handoff Card
user: Families and small teams coordinating across calendar ecosystems who need a dependable, copyable event handoff when an invite is missed, blocked, or inconvenient to open.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A parent seeking a simple self-hostable shared calendar across Android and iOS says the problem is too many projects to test rather than a lack of calendar options.
A request for plain-text event copy says attendees miss invites through spam or forget them, then ask for details through email, WhatsApp, or Telegram.

recurrence: Both requests show calendar interoperability fails at the handoff point: recipients need one simple representation rather than another calendar migration.
current_workaround: Forward an ICS file, screenshot the event, manually type the time/meeting link into chat, or ask everyone to join the same calendar service.
incumbents_and_gap: Google Calendar and Nextcloud can share events, while family calendar apps centralize planning; none focuses on a privacy-preserving, channel-ready card that preserves timezone and RSVP details without an account.
smallest_useful_product: A local web tool that accepts pasted event fields or an ICS file and creates accessible plain text, a compact image/PDF card, timezone equivalents, joining details, and a minimal add-to-calendar link. Non-goals: calendar sync, event hosting, invitations, or contact storage.
success_measure: In a pilot, 80% of recipients can identify the correct local time and joining link from the shared card without opening an ICS file; senders create a card in under 60 seconds.
monetization: free — frictionless sharing and no-account privacy are central; a paid white-label embed can be considered only after organic use.
constraints: Perform ICS parsing in-browser; make event links and descriptions opt-in in QR/image output; handle DST/timezone conversion deterministically; no tracking pixels.
why_distinct: It is a calendar interoperability handoff format, not another scheduling or shared-calendar product.
